It's hard to say which to go for first, as they are totally different despite both being strategy. Civ is more about creating and controlling an empire and acquiring resources, exploring new lands, and growing cities with the allocation of said resources. The Total War series, on the other hand, is more about placing the player in the position of all-seeing commander of historical forces, and though it does feature some empire and resource management, it is much lighter on those fronts than Civ.

So in answer to your question, it depends basically whether you want to be a politician or a general. In both games, you will play each role, but Civ is much more about making you the King, Emperor, etc., and Total War much more about being the General.

Civilization and Total War are very different games. They are both strategy games in the sense that Contra and Call of Duty are both shooters.

Generally speaking, there are roughly two main ways to categorize most Strategy games. The lines are ambiguous, but important.

First, is the game Turn-based or Real-Time? Generally speaking, turn-based games tend to focus on slower and more deliberate strategies, while real-time games emphasize management and quick decision-making. Second, is the emphasis on Tactics or Grand Strategy? Tactics typically focuses on using a pre-determined set of units and resources, while Grand Strategy focuses largely on the preparations for the battles and circumstances surrounding them.

The Total War series is odd because it is basically two games in one. The core of the game is managing the Grand Strategy of a large empire in a turn-based fashion. However, when you enter battles, you enter smaller real-time tactical fights. The emphasis is slightly more on the Grand Strategy, especially since you pick which battles to fight on a one-by-one basis.

The following are some of the better games in each subgenre.

Turn-Based Grand Strategy: Civilization 3/4/5

Turn-Based Tactics: XCOM, Valkyria Chronicles

Real-time Grand Strategy: Age of Empires 2, Starcraft, Warcraft 3.

Real-Time Tactics: Company of Heroes, Blizkrieg

The author of this video starts off with a blatantly wrong assumption about genes and natural selection. That is, the notion that selection occurs in a eco-battlefield where "survival of the fittest" is the primary determinant of genetic success. It's more than a mere oversimplification. It's a term Darwin never used. Regardless, if it were true why would sharks remain nearly unchanged for hundreds of millions of years? Or spiders? Or ants? Or mollusks? Etc etc etc. It goes on. There are long periods of steady-state where natural selection merely shifts minor aspects of a larger biomorphic plan. This is not because sharks (or what have you) are at some pinnacle of an evolutionary ladder. Or food chain. Or some other metaphor for "best". It is random.

That's right. Entirely random. The environment where these animals evolved to steady-state didn't shift. So, by chance, across eons the organisms remained the same too.

The problem with this guy's argument is that he's using ideas about evolutionary biology taken from a video game to support his thesis. The one academic source he cited, Dawkins' The Selfish Gene doesn't really deal with memes. That's a minor digression in a book otherwise devoted to arguing against group selection. That book was directed at Harvard's Stephen Jay Gould and his group selection theory. Which, BTW: no matter how popular Dawkins is due to his popularizing atheism, Gould won that fight on a factual basis. The Selfish Gene is an interesting and entertaining book. But it's not taken seriously in evolutionary biology circles.

OK, so the notion that memes on the internet can propagate crazy ideas because the norms of natural selection for ideas have broken down is also completely false. On two grounds. One, being that false and crazy ideas have been propagated throughout history without the Internet. Just look at creation myths across world cultures, for example. Secondly, it's based on a false notion of biological evolution as a model for memetic information propagation through culture - as discussed previously.

Therefore, his argument relies on two foundational assertions that can be clearly and obviously proved false. Thus the argument fails. Badly.

(and he doesn't even try to address biological parasites and the relation to parasitic ideas).

Please see: Douglas Hofstadter's Metamagical Themas for a much more rigorous discussion of memes and memetic information transfer through culture.

Did Metal Gear Solid 2 Really Foreshadow SJW Culture?

It's a great video, with a cogent point. While I think Kojima wasn't predicting specifically the rise of SJW's and PC culture way back in 2001, instead he was predicting the core characteristics that are common to information distribution in the digital age, and how such info can be manipulated. The video above touches on this, applying the framework of information curation and manipulation that was Kojima's thesis in MGS2 to the current SJW phenomenon.

In reality I think the problems Kojima set out in MGS2 are far bigger than mere SJW idiocy. Kojima showed us, as Orwell did, as Bradbury did and as Gibson did, how fragile the 'truth' is. How easily it is for those with any kind of authority or power to use information for their own ends, while simultaneously using it as a weapon against their enemies. One of Kojima's points is that today, we have too much information. Every person is continuously, relentlessly bombarded with junk information - Facebook, buzzfeed, Twitter, reddit and a million other sources - that any kind of sense of importance is lost. There is no filter anymore and as such the public drowns in white noise, unable to truly engage with any kind of important information. It's why when it was revealed the Chicago PD operated a fucking blacksite in their own city, detaining people without any legal authority, it was minor news. Few people saw the story, fewer cared. The populous was distracted by the deluge of puff pieces about everything from the NFL to Miley Cyrus.

We live in an age where everyone has a voice, and it seems like nothing of importance can be heard. I think more than SJW's, Kojima was warning us how the abundance of information was a threat to democracy and a weapon of totalitarianism. The worst thing was, he was right.

SJWs are just an effect of this awful information shit fest that the internet has turned into. But it will allow people like social justice warriors, who do what the video said they do, to thrive over the ones who aren't as interested in those things.

We saw it with reddit too. Reddit, a long, long time ago, used to be an absolutely awesome place filled with quality articles and comments that were equally amazing. And now look at it. It's complete shit compared to how it was. Instead of quality discussion, you get a bunch of people struggling to make jokes and puns for internet points.

People aren't adjusting to all this information we have. They don't generally have the will power to avoid click bait and the useless stuff and spend their time learning and improving themselves. The internet is a vast library with the most information gathered that humanity has ever gathered. The greatest libraries of all time hold just a portion of what a website like Wikipedia holds. And so many people feel compelled to spend their time in places like Gawker, Reddit, Facebook, etc digesting useless information while ignoring good information, and pushing that useless information forward.

A handgun is something that needs to fit you. The grips need to physically fit your hands, the sights need to be suitable for your eyes, the balance needs to feel right, and the trigger reach and trigger angle needs to work for your finger. The amount of kick it has, or doesn't have, is important too.

There are dozens of really nice pistols that meet your general requirements. The way to find the right one for you is to find a range that has pistols available for rent and try them out. You'll probably fall in love with something that you wouldn't even consider if you had to choose now.

Here are two tips for making sure a pistol fits your hands:

1) Check the pistol once more to be sure that it is empty. Pick a spot on the wall that you can safely point the gun at. Hold the gun in a comfortable one-handed grip, pointed at the floor, stare at the spot for a moment, and close your eyes. Raise the pistol and aim it at where you remember the spot to be. Now open your eyes.

Chances are, the gun will be pointed to the left or the right of the spot, even though your hand is it pointed where you want it. Sometimes the gun is pointed too high or too low. This gun does not fit your hand and you will be fighting it every day.

It does not need to be perfect, but it needs to be close. If you have to adjust your wrist to make the gun happy, it's wrong.

2) If the gun passes the first test, keep your eyes open and aim for the middle of the spot. Now tighten your grip. Does the gun move around? That's bad. A little trembling is OK but it should not shift around.

While you are at it, how does the trigger pull feel? Is your finger too high or too low on the trigger? Does the spot between the middle of your first digit and the first joint fit nice and flat over the face of the trigger? Can you pull the trigger straight back towards your eye in a natural motion?

Are the sights big and clear and obvious? Do you have to hunt around to find the front sight, or is it just right there where you expect it?

When you shoot the gun, if it kicks too hard get something smaller. Do to otherwise is a sure way to develop bad habits that are tough to break. Once you master a smaller gun you can always move up later. Most of us started on .22s, and that's really the best way.

Most people find that revolvers fit them best, because unlike auto pistols revolvers accept a wide range of different-sized grips. However, if you want a pistol, there are many choices and the chances are you can find exactly what you want.

I breezed through the comments and for the most part you have been given some good and solid advice. Of course, I still have to add my $.02 here. I see many, many posts just like yours all over forums and I have a little internal battle every time.

My first inclination, simply from reading your initial post, is you're not quite there yet (what Kromulent said.) I'm also going to pound more of the same from other comments: go and shoot as many makes/models you can get your hands on. Whether it's at the range or some that friends have. Stop focusing on price and work more on finding a weapon/style that fits you. And one you can handle and fire consistently. I've seen too many young men jump right in to the 1911 because it was 'cool' or someone advised them that was the way to go. Then they find out that it isn't like TV - - they can't hit a damn thing at 20 ft and then realize they don't know how to tear it down and maintain. Ends up being a waste of money. You really need to build proficiency before you run out and buy a weapon and CC. Shoot, shoot, shoot. Try lots of models out. Get some training - - even if it's just from some old timers. Then save your $ and get what you want.

All that said, and just so I at least answer the root of your question, here are a couple I suggest: * Springfield XDS - Beautiful single stacker. You can get a 9mm 3.3 that is fantastic for CC. * Glock G26 - Glock is arguably one of the most reliable weapons on the planet. Lots of options in the compact and sub-compact arena. * Ruger SR9 - It's a Ruger. Small, light and reliable. * Taurus Millenium G2 - Really not a bad weapon but my least favorite of the ones I listed. You just never know what fits a person though and it's worth a look.

Those are just a couple that should get you going in the right direction. And yes, I picked all 9mm for you. Start there. You can go to 10mm or .40, even .45, but I just don't recommend for a beginner. The 9mm is an excellent caliber and is very manageable. The bigger calibers in sub-compact frames are just not that easy to shoot and maintain accuracy - target acquisition after the first shot is critical and you'll find yourself in much better shape at 9mm.

Only my opinions. Most importantly, be smart, be safe and be sure.
